title: 2 Chronicles 31:1–10
context: After the Passover, the people go out through Judah and Benjamin, and also Ephraim and Manasseh, and destroy the pillars, Asherah poles, high places, and altars before returning home. Hezekiah restores the divisions of priests and Levites, gives from his own possessions for the regular burnt offerings, and commands the people of Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and Levites so they can devote themselves to the LORD’s law (compare Numbers 18:21). The people respond with abundant first fruits and tithes, piled in heaps from the third month to the seventh, and Azariah the chief priest reports that there has been enough to eat with plenty left over because the LORD has blessed his people. Readers in both traditions commonly treat the passage as shared ground about generous giving, support for those who serve in God’s house, and gratitude for God’s blessing. The reform is broader than the brief notice of Hezekiah’s removals in 2 Kings 18:4.

verses.text: Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke the pillars in pieces, cut down the Asherah poles, and broke down the high places and the altars out of all Judah and Benjamin, also in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the children of Israel returned, every man to his possession, into their own cities.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people destroying pillars, Asherah poles, high places, and altars throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Worship leads to practical reform.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the removal of idolatry as the fruit of renewed covenant faithfulness (compare 2 Kings 18:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that true worship changes how people live.

verses.text: Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and the Levites after their divisions, every man according to his service, both the priests and the Levites, for burnt offerings and for peace offerings, to minister, to give thanks, and to praise in the gates of the LORD’s camp.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah appointing the divisions of priests and Levites for offerings, thanks, and praise. Ordered service supports ongoing worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reorganization as restoring God’s appointed order. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as valuing structure in the service of God.

verses.text: He also appointed the king’s portion of his possessions for the burnt offerings: for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, for the new moons, and for the set feasts, as it is written in the LORD’s law.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king giving from his own possessions for the regular burnt offerings. Leadership includes generous giving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s provision as following what is written in the LORD’s law. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an example of leaders supporting worship personally.

verses.text: Moreover he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion of the priests and the Levites, that they might give themselves to the LORD’s law.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah commanding the people of Jerusalem to give the portion of the priests and Levites. Support enables them to devote themselves to God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the provision as rooted in God’s design for supporting those who serve (compare Numbers 18:21; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a principle of caring for those who minister.

verses.text: As soon as the commandment went out, the children of Israel gave in abundance the first fruits of grain, new wine, oil, honey, and of all the increase of the field; and they brought in the tithe of all things abundantly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people giving abundantly of first fruits and tithes as soon as the command went out. Willing hearts respond generously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundant giving as the fruit of hearts renewed by God (compare Proverbs 3:9). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of generous response to God.

verses.text: The children of Israel and Judah, who lived in the cities of Judah, also brought in the tithe of cattle and sheep, and the tithe of dedicated things which were consecrated to the LORD their God, and laid them in heaps.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people of Israel and Judah bringing tithes of cattle, sheep, and dedicated things, piled in heaps. Giving is shared across the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heaps as visible evidence of God’s blessing and the people’s gratitude. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating cheerful generosity (compare 2 Corinthians 9:7).

verses.text: In the third month, they began to lay the foundation of the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the heaps begun in the third month and finished in the seventh. Generosity continues over a long season.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sustained giving as faithfulness that endures beyond initial enthusiasm. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing steady devotion.

verses.text: When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah and the princes blessing the LORD and his people when they see the heaps. Gratitude flows to God and to the givers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the blessing as recognizing God as the source of all abundance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of thankful leadership.

verses.text: Then Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah asking the priests and Levites about the heaps. He seeks to understand and manage the abundance wisely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his questions as responsible stewardship of what has been given. Both traditions commonly read the verse as care for good administration.

verses.text: Azariah the chief priest, of the house of Zadok, answered him and said, “Since people began to bring the offerings into the LORD’s house, we have eaten and had enough, and have plenty left over, for the LORD has blessed his people; and that which is left is this great store.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Azariah reporting that there has been enough to eat with plenty left over because the LORD has blessed his people. Faithful giving brings blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundance as God’s gracious provision, not a reward earned by giving. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as gratitude for God’s goodness (compare Malachi 3:10).
